newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Kohl, SPD start German tax reform "summit".
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Kohl, SPD start German tax reform "summit".

text.p: Germany's ruling parties and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) met on Monday for a crunch tax summit to try to find a quick fix for record unemployment and get state finances into shape for European monetary union.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl and SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine met to discuss a coalition plan to cut 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in taxes to boost job creation after Germany's January unemployment hit 4.7 million -- the highest since 1933.
The unusual meeting between Kohl and Lafontaine is part of a round of high-stakes poker ahead of 1998 elections and the start of European monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
Unemployment and failing tax revenues are jeopardising Bonn's bid to reduce its budget deficit this year below the ceiling of three percent of GDP specified in EMU's guiding Maastricht treaty.
Failure to reach agreement would condemn long overdue tax reforms to a tortuous path through parliament, where they could fall prey to the SPD's upper house majority.
Kohl made no predictions before the meeting, saying only: "This is a first working meeting. Both sides must put their cards on the table."
Christian Democrat (CDU) general secretary Peter Hintze urged the SPD to reach a compromise on crucial tax reforms by Easter so it could be put into law and implemented from the start of next year.

"By Easter we must have clarity over whether the SPD...is really ready to work with us on tax reforms or just revert to its blocking strategy," Hintze told reporters after a meeting of CDU leaders approved the party's negotiating position.
"There will not be a reform at any price and we will not allow the reforms to be talked to death," he said.
Lafontaine said the SPD wanted to link a drop in unit labour costs with an "ecological tax reform" that would bring higher taxes on energy and promote environmental technology.
Kohl's proposal to cut higher tax brackets but take away tax benefits from employees working unsocial hours was unjust and would do nothing to boost domestic demand, he added.
"It makes no sense to cut burdens on average incomes and then offset them with additional burdens," he said.
Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of Kohl's Free Democrat (FDP) junior coalition partners, called the meeting "one of the last big chances for politicians to win the battle against unemployment."
Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax proposals foresee big cuts in income and corporate tax rates over the next two years, offset in part by abolishing over 70 tax breaks.

The SPD has said it was willing to compromise on some measures, but opposes Waigel's plan to cut the top income tax rate to 39 percent from 53 percent. It hardened its rhetoric ahead of the summit, saying the tax reforms must benefit normal wage earners by cutting non-wage costs.

"We are obliged to help the nation, not the government," SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping told ZDF public television. He said he wanted to "create order, reduce the burdens on citizens, to revive the economy -- but not to perfume a pile of manure."
In a separate radio interview, Scharping said Waigel's plans would tear a 50 billion mark hole in the budget.
"In a nation with 4.7 million unemployed, we cannot afford to waste time or be unclear about the issues," he said.
Monday's talks were unlikely to bring quick results, but if they start well they could set in motion a deal-making process which would circumvent lengthy parliamentary wrangling.
Analysts at Deutsche Bank Research said in a research note on Monday a compromise was in sight and signs were increasing that key parts of the reform could be brought forward to 1998.
"It would be better to bring the whole reform forward to 1998. That could, however, endanger the credibility of the process of consolidating public finances," Deutsche Bank said.
It added: "The less the whole tax reform is watered down and the quicker it is cleared up, the sooner we can expect impulses for the economy."
($ = 1.676 German Marks)
